claims.text: Controlled thermal annealing can enhance surface segregation in HEA nanoparticles.
Annealing-induced surface segregation reduces the cohesive energy at the nanoparticle surface.
Reduced surface cohesive energy lowers the onset temperature for premelting relative to a chemically homogeneous surface.
The proposed initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a largely homogeneous elemental distribution.
The proposed nanoparticles are in the 5–20 nm size range.
Varying annealing temperature and time can produce controlled degrees of surface segregation while preserving overall composition.
Heating AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles produces an AuCu-enriched layer at their surface.
Au and Cu are lower-cohesion elements in the relevant HEA surface environment.
Temperature-dependent phase separation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles is driven by pronounced atomic diffusion.
The segregated surface layer has lower surface energy and weaker local bonding than a homogeneous surface.
A segregated surface layer begins surface premelting earlier than a chemically homogeneous nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation effectively decouples surface melting from bulk melting.
Nanoparticles annealed to induce significant surface segregation will have a lower premelting onset temperature than minimally segregated controls.
Nanoparticles retaining a homogeneous surface composition will have higher premelting onset temperatures.
The proposed segregation effect should hold for nanoparticles between 5 and 20 nm.
The proposed segregation effect should extend to HEA systems with compositions similar to AuCoCuNiPt.
The magnitude of the premelting-temperature shift depends on elemental-diffusion kinetics and the specific HEA composition.
Atomic diffusion in heated AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles is more active than in corresponding monometallic and bimetallic subsystems.
